issues.legal_issue: A developer’s promise to endeavour to complete a housing unit by a stipulated time requires reasonable efforts to meet that time and cannot leave possession to the developer’s indefinite discretion.
material_facts: A standard-form allotment letter stated that the developer would endeavour to complete the dwelling unit within two and a half years.
The unit was not completed and possession was not offered within that period.
The buyer had applied for the unit and received an allotment under the standard-form terms.
issues.conclusion: The promise required the developer to make all reasonable efforts to hand over possession by the stipulated time; it did not give the developer indefinite discretion. The developer bore the burden of explaining the steps it took to comply.
issues.legal_principle: The contractual expression “endeavour” must be construed in the context of the whole clause and the parties’ obligations. It requires an earnest, reasonable effort to meet the stipulated time. A contrary interpretation would leave the purchaser at the developer’s mercy. The developer must explain the steps taken to comply with the contractual stipulation.

predicates.consumer_appeal: A developer appealed an order made in a consumer dispute concerning a housing purchase.
predicates.developer_promised_endeavours_by_stipula: A developer promised in the allotment terms to endeavour to complete the unit within a stated time.
predicates.possession_was_delayed: The developer did not hand over possession within the stipulated time.

issues.definition: When a consumer appeal concerns delayed possession under a promise to endeavour to meet a stated time, the developer must make reasonable efforts to meet that time.

issues.legal_issue: A consumer forum may award just and reasonable compensation for delayed possession notwithstanding a one-sided contractual limit on the developer’s liability.
material_facts: The allotment terms were in a standard form that the purchaser had no practical choice but to sign.
The terms limited the developer’s compensation for delay to a low per-area amount, while requiring substantially higher interest from the purchaser for delayed instalments.
The developer delayed handing over possession, and the consumer commission awarded compensation above the contractual amount.
issues.conclusion: The contractual compensation term was one-sided and constituted an unfair trade practice; it did not constrain the consumer forum from awarding just and reasonable compensation for the delay.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 2(1)(r) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, incorporating one-sided terms in this kind of standard-form agreement may constitute an unfair trade practice. Under Section 2(1)(o), housing construction is a service, and a failure to provide possession within the contractual period may amount to a deficiency in service. Section 14(1)(e) empowers a consumer forum to direct removal of that deficiency, including by awarding compensation as restitution. The Court relied on Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Limited v. Govindan Raghavan and Wg. Cdr. Arifur Rahman Khan v. DLF Southern Homes Pvt. Ltd.; it also noted that, although parties are ordinarily held to their bargain as discussed in Dhanda, that does not make an unfair term controlling in these circumstances.

rule.if: consumer_appeal and developer_used_standard_form_agreement and purchaser_had_no_real_choice and developer_delay_compensation_was_less_favourable_than_purchaser_default_terms and possession_was_delayed

predicates.consumer_appeal: A developer appealed an order made in a consumer dispute concerning a housing purchase.
predicates.developer_used_standard_form_agreement: A developer used a standard-form agreement for the housing purchase.
predicates.purchaser_had_no_real_choice: The purchaser had no practical choice but to accept the developer’s agreement terms.
predicates.developer_delay_compensation_was_less_fa: The agreement imposed a substantially less favourable consequence on the developer for delay than on the purchaser for delayed payment.
predicates.possession_was_delayed: The developer did not hand over possession within the contractual period.

issues.definition: Where a developer appeals in a delayed-possession consumer dispute involving a no-choice standard-form agreement with materially unequal consequences, the consumer forum may award just and reasonable delay compensation.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for delayed possession must reflect the contractual grace period and be set at a reasonable rate in light of prevailing market conditions.
material_facts: The allotment terms allowed two and a half years for completion and contemplated a further one-year period before compensation became payable, apart from valid force majeure extensions.
The consumer commission awarded interest from before that further period had expired and at a rate the Supreme Court found excessive in light of prevailing market conditions.
The dwelling unit was ultimately handed over to the purchaser.
issues.conclusion: The Court modified the compensation award to simple interest at 7% per annum from 1 January 2016 until possession was handed over on 26 July 2018, rather than the 10% awarded from July 2015.
issues.legal_principle: The allotment clause, read as a whole, indicated a completion period of two and a half years followed by a one-year period before compensation became payable; the inconsistent reference to four years did not displace that reading. The rate must be reasonable in light of prevailing market conditions. The Court relied on Central Bank of India v. Ravindra, (2002) 1 SCC 367, paragraph 39, in assessing the rate.

predicates.consumer_appeal: A developer appealed an order made in a consumer dispute concerning a housing purchase.
predicates.contractual_completion_period_and_grace_: The allotment terms stated a period for completion and an additional period before delay compensation became payable.
predicates.possession_was_delayed_beyond_those_peri: The developer handed over possession only after the completion and additional periods had passed.
predicates.consumer_commission_awarded_delay_intere: The consumer commission awarded interest as compensation for delayed possession.

issues.definition: When delayed possession extends beyond stated completion and grace periods and a consumer commission has awarded interest, the interest must begin after the contractual grace period and be set at a reasonable rate.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser cannot receive a separate award for loss of rent in addition to interest that compensates for the same delay in handing over possession.
material_facts: The consumer commission awarded interest for the delayed handover of the dwelling unit.
It also awarded a separate amount for loss of rent arising from the delay.
issues.conclusion: The separate award for loss of rent was set aside because the interest award already compensated the purchaser for the delayed handover.
issues.legal_principle: Where interest has been awarded as compensation for delayed possession, an additional award for loss of rent arising from that same delay is not justified.

predicates.consumer_appeal: A developer appealed an order made in a consumer dispute concerning a housing purchase.
predicates.delay_interest_compensates_for_late_poss: A consumer commission awarded interest to compensate a purchaser for delayed possession.
predicates.separate_loss_of_rent_compensation_was_a: The consumer commission separately awarded the purchaser loss-of-rent compensation for that same delay.

issues.definition: If interest compensates for late possession and a separate loss-of-rent award compensates for the same delay, the separate award must be set aside.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser’s delayed instalment does not defeat compensation for delayed possession where the developer itself could not deliver possession when the relevant payment was expected to fall due.
material_facts: The purchaser paid the fifth instalment after its scheduled due date.
The final instalment was payable when the possession letter was issued, which was expected around the time the developer had undertaken to complete the unit.
The developer was not in a position to hand over possession by that expected time.
The purchaser had paid more than one crore rupees out of the total sale consideration.
issues.conclusion: The developer’s argument that the purchaser’s delay in paying the fifth instalment justified denying interest was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The instalment obligation must be assessed in light of the developer’s own ability to perform. Where the developer could not deliver possession when it was expected to do so, the earlier instalment requirement cannot be used to defeat compensation for the developer’s delay.

rule.if: consumer_appeal and purchaser_paid_an_instalment_late and final_payment_was_tied_to_possession and developer_could_not_deliver_possession_when_expected

predicates.consumer_appeal: A developer appealed an order made in a consumer dispute concerning a housing purchase.
predicates.purchaser_paid_an_instalment_late: A purchaser paid an instalment after its scheduled due date.
predicates.final_payment_was_tied_to_possession: The final payment was due when possession was offered or the possession letter was issued.
predicates.developer_could_not_deliver_possession_w: The developer was not in a position to hand over possession at the time it was expected to do so.

issues.definition: When a purchaser paid an instalment late but the final payment depended on possession and the developer could not deliver possession when expected, the late instalment does not defeat delay compensation.

issues.legal_issue: Routine business or construction difficulties do not qualify as force majeure where an experienced developer should have anticipated them.
material_facts: The developer relied on a dispute with its contractor concerning termination and a boundary-wall dispute with neighbouring landowners to explain the delay.
The developer was experienced and the asserted difficulties were routine business exigencies.
The developer did not establish a qualifying force majeure event that excused its delay.
issues.conclusion: The force majeure defence was rejected, and the developer remained liable for compensation for delayed possession.
issues.legal_principle: Ordinary and foreseeable delays arising from business exigencies do not frustrate the contract or absolve a developer of its obligations under a force majeure clause. The Court relied on DLF Home Developers Ltd. v. Capital Greens Flat Buyers Association, which treated routine project delays as insufficient grounds for such a defence.

predicates.consumer_appeal: A developer appealed an order made in a consumer dispute concerning a housing purchase.
predicates.developer_invoked_force_majeure: A developer relied on force majeure to excuse delayed possession.
predicates.asserted_delay_arose_from_routine_or_for: The asserted causes of delay were ordinary or foreseeable difficulties associated with the developer’s business or construction project.

issues.definition: If a developer invokes force majeure for delayed possession but relies on routine or foreseeable business difficulties, that defence does not excuse the delay.
